sources.news_title: Trump Secures Release of American Imprisoned in Russia
sources.text:
Trump Secures Release of American Imprisoned in Russia
President Donald Trump has secured the release of an American citizen who spent more than four years in Russian custody, following a personal appeal to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Stephen James Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired English teacher from Michigan, was released Wednesday after Trump reportedly raised his case directly with Putin during a telephone conversation last week. Hubbard had been imprisoned since 2022 on charges that American officials and his family strongly disputed.
The release came during a diplomatic meeting in St. Petersburg between Putin and U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, who traveled to Russia for discussions concerning the ongoing war in Ukraine. Russian officials described the decision as a humanitarian gesture, citing Hubbard’s age, deteriorating health, and Trump’s personal involvement.
Hubbard, originally from Big Rapids, Michigan, had been living in Izyum, Ukraine, since 2014. Before settling there, he spent years working as an English teacher in Japan and Cyprus.
Russian forces detained Hubbard in April 2022, shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Authorities accused him of joining Ukrainian military operations as a mercenary.
Prosecutors alleged that Hubbard had signed a military contract, received weapons training, and participated in combat activities. A Russian court convicted him during closed proceedings in October 2024, sentencing him to six years and ten months.
His relatives consistently rejected those accusations, maintaining that Hubbard was a civilian with no military involvement. Family members said Russian personnel had taken him from his residence.
The U.S. State Department officially classified Hubbard as wrongfully detained in January 2025, recognizing serious concerns surrounding his imprisonment and prosecution.
Concerns about Hubbard’s physical condition intensified during his detention, with relatives expressing fears that his health was worsening while he remained in Russian custody.
According to Russian officials, Putin personally informed Witkoff of the decision to release Hubbard. The American was subsequently transported to Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg to begin his journey home.
Witkoff thanked Putin for the humanitarian decision and briefly met with Hubbard before his departure. The former prisoner reportedly expressed gratitude toward those responsible for negotiating his freedom.
Hubbard’s attorney, Martin De Luca, said his client was extremely happy about the development, although his physical condition remained fragile following years of imprisonment.
Trump celebrated the announcement on Truth Social, writing:
“Stephen Hubbard, taken four years ago by Russia during the Biden Administration, was just released from prison, at the request of President Donald J. Trump, made directly to President Vladimir Putin in a telephone conversation last week. Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family.”
The president emphasized that the United States had not been required to release another prisoner or provide concessions in exchange for Hubbard’s freedom.
“The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release. This major return should have taken place long ago through the Biden Administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin,” Trump added.
Trump also welcomed Hubbard’s return, stating, “Welcome home Stephen, it’s great to have you back.”
The president suggested that his administration’s decision to delay additional sanctions against Russia helped preserve the diplomatic discussions. He argued that imposing new penalties could have disrupted negotiations surrounding Hubbard’s release.
Hubbard’s son, Joseph Coleman, expressed the family’s appreciation for the efforts of both Trump and Putin. Although other Americans reportedly remain detained in Russia, Hubbard was the last American prisoner in the country formally designated as wrongfully detained by the State Department at the time of his release.

Russia released a US prisoner. What did they get out of it?
How Donald Trump is making Russia’s month, briefly explained.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is cozying up to Russia again.
What’s happening? On Wednesday, Russia released an American prisoner, 74-year-old retired teacher Stephen Hubbard, back to the US. The US, Trump said in a social media post, “out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return.”
Hubbard’s release is unquestionably good news. But Trump is wrong: In just the last month, his administration has delivered for Russia in more ways than one, often inexplicably and despite bipartisan condemnation.
What is Trump doing for Russia? Late last week, he waived upcoming economic sanctions on Russia that he had only recently signed into law after they passed Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support. He also:
- Struck a diesel deal with Russia, temporarily lifting fuel sanctions on the country in exchange for Russia releasing a trivial amount of diesel into the global market;
- Announced — seemingly without talking to either party — a Russia-Ukraine “energy ceasefire” favorable to Russia (which has since fallen apart);
- Temporarily interrupted US intel sharing with Ukraine and played a role in interfering with Ukraine’s access to Starlink, which helps power the country’s drone warfare against Russia; and
- Called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced.
Last month, Trump also invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the annual G20 summit later this year, which would mark Putin’s first appearance since 2019.
What does Trump get out of all of this? There’s Hubbard’s release, but taking that on Trump’s own terms (muddled though they are), the US didn’t give anything to secure it — which means that all of those favors have amounted to not much at all, other than papering over Russia’s role as an international bad actor and breaking with US allies in Europe.
Why does this matter? Trump’s Russia embrace comes at an awful time for Ukraine, which, as the New York Times reported earlier this month, is facing a Russian campaign to “freeze Ukrainians into submission” as winter approaches. Nevertheless, on Wednesday, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian.”

Sister of American Stephen Hubbard says he's in disbelief following release by Russia
sources.text:
DENVER (AP) — The younger sister of Stephen Hubbard, the American freed Wednesday after spending more than four years in a Russian prison, said she spoke with her brother by phone and described him as being in disbelief.
“That was awesome. He was just laughing. ... He said, ‘I can’t believe this is happening,'" Patricia Hubbard Fox told The Associated Press in a phone interview as she headed to Denver's airport to catch a flight to San Antonio to meet her brother.
President Donald Trump said he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call earlier this month to free Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan. Hubbard was headed home following a visit to St. Petersburg by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who also held talks with Putin about the war in Ukraine.
“He’s out of Russia territory. He is free, praise God. He really thought he was going to die in prison,” Hubbard Fox said, adding that her brother suffered beatings and starvation while he was held captive.
She said her brother was in perfect health when he was “kidnapped” in 2022 and accused of fighting alongside Kyiv's forces. She said he now suffers from an enlarged heart and likely has post-traumatic stress disorder.
Her brother was accused of signing a contract with the Ukrainian military and sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison during closed court proceedings. The U.S. government under the Biden administration designated him as wrongfully detained, and his legal team has also disputed the Russian allegation, saying he was not involved in any military activity.
Hubbard, a U.S. Air Force veteran, taught English overseas and retired in 2012 to Cyprus, where one of his sons is an Orthodox Christian priest. He later moved to Ukraine to be with a woman he had met, his lawyers said, and remained in the country after the relationship ended and was living there at the time of Russia’s invasion.
Hubbard Fox also disputed the claim that her brother was a mercenary, saying he was used as “bait” in Putin's war with Ukraine.
“Putin is as evil as they come,” she said.
Hubbard Fox said her brother would probably come live with her in Colorado, and they both were looking forward to a family reunion. And perhaps she will be able to get some peaceful sleep in her own bed.
Hubbard Fox said she has slept on her couch for four years in solidarity with her brother “because I figured he didn’t have a bed. Why should I have a bed?”

Russia on Wednesday freed an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, a deal completed during a visit by a top U.S. envoy and at a time when President Donald Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Moscow.
Trump told reporters at the White House that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin during a recent call to free Stephen Hubbard and that, unlike previous releases, the U.S. did not have to give up anyone in return.
“He is the happiest man around,” Trump said of Hubbard, describing the 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan as a “very high-quality, innocent man.”
Hubbard’s release occurred during a visit to St. Petersburg by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who in a face-to-face interaction with Putin praised the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” as the men held talks about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and as Trump simultaneously pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Hubbard, who before his arrest had lived in Ukraine for years, was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison during closed court proceedings. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia’s invasion in 2022, and that he fought alongside Kyiv’s forces until being captured two months later.
The U.S. government under President Joe Biden’s administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained, and his legal team and family have disputed the Russian allegation, saying he was not involved in any military activity.
“He was just for bait. It was all about bait. And that’s why they kidnap Americans,” his sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, said in an interview with The Associated Press. She said she expected Hubbard to stay with her in Colorado.
“Steven James Hubbard is the face of America,” she said. “They could do that to anybody. They just happened to see him. ‘Oh, that’s an American, let’s go get him.’”
Witkoff, a key Trump administration figure who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February 2027, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he’s going home to his family.”
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media Wednesday that Hubbard’s release was “raised by the American side for a certain time,” and Putin decided to free the man out of “humanitarian considerations.”
Speaking to reporters after the talks, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said the Kremlin leader had pardoned Hubbard, who upon his release was taken to St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo airport for Witkoff to bring him home to the United States.
Video showed Witkoff and Hubbard shaking hands, with the newly released American thanking the envoy. Witkoff introduced Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev to Hubbard and described him as someone “who had a lot to do with this happening.”
“We just met President Putin, he sends you blessings and wishes you good things,” Witkoff added.
Hubbard, a U.S. Air Force veteran, taught English overseas and retired in 2012 to Cyprus, where one of his sons is a Christian Orthodox priest. He later moved to Ukraine to be with a woman he had met, his lawyers said, remaining in the country after the relationship ended and living there at the time of Russia’s 2022 invasion.
His case was taken up by lawyers at the U.S.-based law firm of Boies Schiller Flexner and the Russian firm of EPAM Law, which together had represented Marc Fogel, the American teacher freed from Russian custody last year, and worked for his release.
“They thought they weren’t going to see him again alive, and Stephen didn’t think he was going to come out of there alive,” Martin De Luca, one of Hubbard’s lawyers at the Boies Schiller firm, said in an interview about Hubbard’s family. “Obviously, they’re overjoyed, but they feel very much like it’s a miracle.”
His sister said she had spoken with Hubbard after his release. “He was just laughing. He said, ‘I can’t believe this is happening,’” Hubbard Fox said of her brother.
The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin.
Those include Trump’s move last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine.
Named after the late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Moscow’s war. That decision followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg.
Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer.
Other Americans, including some with serious illnesses, remain jailed in Russia. Hubbard was the last remaining American designated as wrongfully detained, although advocates say that label should be applied to other prisoners.
Russia reported more arrests of foreigners in recent days. The FSB security service said Wednesday it detained a German national suspected of mercenary activities and last week announced arrests of a Swedish national suspected of sabotage and a Japanese journalist accused of espionage.

ST. PETERSBURG, Russia — Russia on Wednesday freed a 74-year-old American teacher who had been held for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine, President Donald Trump said, announcing that the release followed his direct request to Russian President Vladimir Putin and required no concessions from the United States.
Stephen Hubbard, a retired teacher from Michigan, was released as U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Putin in St. Petersburg for talks on ending the war in Ukraine. Putin announced the release during the meeting and said Hubbard had been taken to the city’s Pulkovo Airport, according to Russian state media and officials.
Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Hubbard “was just released from prison, at the request of President Donald J. Trump, made directly to President Vladimir Putin in a telephone conversation last week. Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family.”
“The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release,” Trump wrote. He said the return “should have taken place long ago through the Biden administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin.”
“Welcome home Stephen, it’s great to have you back,” Trump wrote.
Witkoff thanked Putin for the release during their meeting, calling him a “humanitarian.”
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff said, according to video and reports from the talks. He later met with Hubbard at the airport.
Hubbard was detained by Russian forces in April 2022 in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izium, where he had been living with a Ukrainian partner, shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion began. A Moscow court convicted him in a closed-door trial in October 2024 of participating as a mercenary and sentenced him to six years and 10 months in prison. Russia on Wednesday freed an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, a deal completed during a visit by a top U.S. envoy and at a time when President Donald Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Moscow.
Trump told reporters at the White House that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin during a recent call to free Stephen Hubbard and that, unlike previous releases, the U.S. did not have to give up anyone in return.
“He is the happiest man around," Trump said of Hubbard, describing the 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan as a “very high-quality, innocent man.” Hubbard's legal team denied the Russian accusations, saying he was not involved in any military activity.
The release occurred during a visit to St. Petersburg by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who in a face-to-face interaction with Putin praised the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” as the men held talks about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and as Trump simultaneously pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Hubbard, who before his arrest had lived in Ukraine for years, was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison during closed court proceedings. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia's invasion in 2022, and that he fought alongside Kyiv's forces until being captured two months later.
The U.S. government under President Joe Biden's administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained. His family also disputed the Russian allegations.
“He was just for bait. It was all about bait. And that’s why they kidnap Americans,” his sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, said in an interview with The Associated Press. She said she expected Hubbard to stay with her in Colorado.
“Steven James Hubbard is the face of America,” she said. “They could do that to anybody. They just happened to see him. ‘Oh, that’s an American, let’s go get him.’”
US envoy calls Putin a ‘humanitarian’
Witkoff, a key Trump administration figure who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February 2027, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he's going home to his family.”
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media Wednesday that Hubbard’s release was “raised by the American side for a certain time,” and Putin decided to free the man out of “humanitarian considerations.”
Speaking to reporters after the talks, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said the Kremlin leader had pardoned Hubbard, who upon his release was taken to St. Petersburg's Pulkovo airport for Witkoff to bring him home to the United States.
Video showed Witkoff and Hubbard shaking hands, with the newly released American thanking the envoy. Witkoff introduced Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev to Hubbard and described him as someone “who had a lot to do with this happening.”
“We just met President Putin, he sends you blessings and wishes you good things,” Witkoff added.
Hubbard, a U.S. Air Force veteran, taught English overseas and retired in 2012 to Cyprus, where one of his sons is an Orthodox Christian priest. He later moved to Ukraine to be with a woman he had met, his lawyers said, remaining in the country after the relationship ended and living there at the time of Russia's 2022 invasion.
His case was taken up by lawyers at the U.S.-based law firm of Boies Schiller Flexner and the Russian firm of EPAM Law, which together had represented Marc Fogel, the American teacher freed from Russian custody last year, and worked for his release.
“They thought they weren't going to see him again alive, and Stephen didn't think he was going to come out of there alive,” Martin De Luca, one of Hubbard's lawyers at the Boies Schiller firm, said in an interview about Hubbard's family. “Obviously, they're overjoyed, but they feel very much like it's a miracle.”
His sister said she had spoken with Hubbard after his release. “He was just laughing. He said, ‘I can’t believe this is happening,’” Hubbard Fox said of her brother.
Other Americans remain jailed in Russia
The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin.
Those include Trump's move last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine.
Named after the late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Moscow’s war. “We just met President Putin, he sends you blessings and wishes you good things,” Witkoff added.
Hubbard, a U.S. Air Force veteran, taught English overseas and retired in 2012 to Cyprus, where one of his sons is a Christian Orthodox priest. He later moved to Ukraine to be with a woman he had met, his lawyers said, remaining in the country after the relationship ended and living there at the time of Russia's 2022 invasion.
His case was taken up by lawyers at the U.S.-based law firm of Boies Schiller Flexner and the Russian firm of EPAM Law, which together had represented Marc Fogel, the American teacher freed from Russian custody last year, and worked for his release.
“They thought they weren't going to see him again alive, and Stephen didn't think he was going to come out of there alive,” Martin De Luca, one of Hubbard's lawyers at the Boies Schiller firm, said in an interview about Hubbard's family. “Obviously, they're overjoyed but they feel very much like it's a miracle.”
Other Americans remain jailed in Russia
The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin.
Those include Trump's move last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after the late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Moscow’s war. That decision followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections.
Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks Wednesday with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg.
Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer.
Other Americans, including some with serious illnesses, remain jailed in Russia. Hubbard was the last remaining American designated as wrongfully detained, although advocates say that label should be applied to other prisoners.
Global Reach, an advocacy group that works to free Americans detained abroad and currently represents five Americans held in Russia, praised the release but called for the other prisoners to come home as well.
“We are grateful to the Trump Administration for reuniting Stephen Hubbard with his family, but at the same time, we know that there are five other families of Americans held in Russia who are going to have a hard time understanding why their loved one was not included in the deal,” Eric Lebson, the group's chief strategy officer, said in a statement.
Hubbard had been imprisoned since 2022 on charges that Hostage Aid Worldwide, a hostage advocacy group, has called bogus.
Russia reported more arrests of foreigners in recent days. The FSB security service said Wednesday it detained a German national suspected of mercenary activities and last week announced arrests of a Swedish national suspected of sabotage and a Japanese journalist accused of espionage.
Tucker reported from Washington; Litvinova reported from Tallinn, Estonia.

Russia releases American Stephen Hubbard after four years in prison
Hubbard was jailed after Russia said he fought alongside Ukrainian forces against Russia.
American Stephen Hubbard has been freed from a Russian prison and is on his way home after United States President Donald Trump said his administration had secured his release.
“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump wrote in a social media post on Wednesday, adding that the US was not required to give anything in return for the release of the 74-year-old former teacher from Michigan.
The deal came during a visit to Russia by a top US envoy, and just days after Trump took a series of actions seen as beneficial to Moscow.
Hubbard, whose family says had been living in Ukraine since before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, was tried and convicted in a closed-door trial, with Russian prosecutors saying he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military and had fought alongside its forces before being captured. He was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2024.
The US had declared Hubbard a wrongfully detained American.
Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is in Russia for talks with President Vladimir Putin on the Ukraine war, told him that “our whole nation sends their thanks” and that Putin was a “humanitarian” for allowing Hubbard to walk free. Witkoff briefly met with Hubbard in St. Petersburg after his release, telling him, “from today is a new life for you”.
The release came at a dynamic moment in relations between the US, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship under strain at the same time that the Trump administration has pursued policies which Ukraine says have rewarded Putin.
Those include Trump’s decision last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that the US Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine.
Named after the late South Carolina Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fuelling Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

sources.news_title: Detained American Stephen Hubbard released by Russia as Witkoff meets Putin - Regional Media News
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Russia on Wednesday to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and oversee the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan who had been in Russian detention since 2022, according to reports in Russian state-run media.
Witkoff landed in the Russian city of St. Petersburg on Wednesday morning, a Kremlin aide confirmed, ahead of the planned meeting with Putin.
Trump’s envoy thanked Putin for freeing Hubbard, according to a readout of the meeting published by the Kremlin. Putin said that Hubbard — who was detained in eastern Ukraine in April 2022 — was taken to St. Peterburg’s Pulkovo Airport, the readout said.
“I want to thank you very much. The president sends his thanks,” Witkoff said, according to the Kremlin readout. “Because of you, he’s going home to his family,” Witkoff added, describing Putin as “a humanitarian.”
Trump later wrote in a post to social media he asked Putin to release Hubbard in a phone call that took place last week. “Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump wrote.
The U.S. “was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia,” Trump added. “There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
The president then posted to social media again defending his recent decision to waive numerous sanctions on Russia. “If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt,” Trump wrote of the discussions over Hubbard’s release.
Witkoff arrived in St. Petersburg as the Trump administration was closing in on a deal that would see multiple Americans released from detention in Russia, two U.S. officials and another source familiar with the matter told ABC News.
The talks were centered on Hubbard and several other U.S. citizens held by Moscow on what the administration believes are dubious charges, the source said.
Hubbard had been living in eastern Ukraine as a civilian since around 2014, where he taught English and had a relationship with a Ukrainian woman, according to his family.
After he was detained, Russian authorities charged Hubbard with acting as a mercenary and fighting for Ukraine, sentencing him to nearly seven years in prison. Hubbard’s family and U.S. officials said the charges were false and the State Department designated him as wrongfully detained.
During their meeting, Witkoff and Putin discussed the latest U.S.-led efforts to end Moscow’s ongoing invasion, which the Kremlin launched in February 2022.
“One thing that I hope to accomplish today is to have some good conversation between us about resumption potentially of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States,” Witkoff said, per the Kremlin readout.
Witkoff also touted U.S.-Russian “business and economic cooperation” as “an example of what the possibilities are in the future.”
Witkoff traveled to St. Petersburg following a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Norwegian capital of Oslo on Tuesday. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also attended the talks, which focused on ceasefire proposals to halt Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Witkoff’s latest round of shuttle diplomacy comes amid intensifying White House pressure on Zelenskyy to make concessions to secure a peace deal with Moscow.
In recent weeks, Trump waived a raft of sanctions on Moscow and again blamed Kyiv for the lack of progress in U.S.-sponsored peace talks, even suggesting that Zelenskyy should be replaced as Ukrainian president.
On Tuesday, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that the U.S. had received “nothing” for its support of Ukraine.
“Look, we have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We’ve got nothing back other than high diesel,” Trump said. “We have given, probably, possibly, more money to Ukraine than almost anybody over the years, hundreds of billions of dollars. We’ve got nothing back, and the American taxpayers are tired of it. We want Zelenskyy to make a deal.”
Following his meetings in Oslo on Tuesday, Zelenskyy said in posts to social media that he was “thankful to the American side” for its input on propose future security guarantees for Kyiv. The Ukrainian president also said he spoke with Secretary of State Marco Rubio by phone to discuss “sensitive issues such as Starlink, ballistic missile interceptors and intelligence.”
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said he continued to hold meetings in Oslo. “A lot depends on whether the American side manages to hear something new from Russia today — about peace, not about continuing the war,” he wrote.
ABC News’ Joe Simonetti, Shannon K. Kingston, Fritz Farrow, Nicholas Kerr, Emily Chang, Patrick Reevell, Anna Sergeeva and Justin Gomez contributed to this report.

US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to consider restarting US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine and explore new solutions to end the ongoing conflict. This ninth face-to-face meeting occurred at a grand palace in St Petersburg, and it began with Russia’s release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher who had been detained. During the meeting, Putin expressed his willingness to assist US President Donald Trump regarding concerns over Iran’s nuclear program and proposed supplying the US with fertilizer to support American farmers. He suggested a potential meeting in China next month that could include Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The discussions come amid worries that the US might be easing its support for Ukraine, including withholding real-time intelligence on Russian military actions. Witkoff noted the need for dialogue about resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States, emphasizing that even a lack of resolution would still be valuable for future steps. The last such peace talks happened in February. Trump has recently pressured Ukraine to negotiate a settlement to avoid dire consequences.
Putin has shown little willingness to change his main objectives, which involve full control of the Donetsk region and preventing Ukraine from joining NATO. Witkoff met with various leaders, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, before these talks, and spoke of successful discussions that presented some momentum. He brought documents with potential peace deal ideas for Putin to consider and mentioned that Jared Kushner would join the talks remotely to share additional proposals.
A US official indicated that Ukraine brought fresh ideas to the Oslo talks, indicating progress toward a coordinated strategy with Russia, which included essential elements for a peace framework such as security guarantees for Ukraine and a post-war economic plan. Zelenskiy expressed hope to discuss critical issues for ending the conflict during a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin. The Kremlin stated any such meeting would require detailed preparations.
US-Ukraine relations have weakened recently, particularly after Trump’s diesel export deal with Russia aimed at reducing fuel costs for Americans amid rising prices linked to conflicts involving Iran. Following this deal, Ukraine reported disruptions in intelligence-sharing and the use of the Starshield military satellite system. Despite these issues, Zelenskiy mentioned that the Oslo meeting led to an agreement to address them. Reports indicated that Elon Musk had slowed down the Starlink satellite service crucial for Ukraine’s tracking of Russian missile strikes. Musk stated that any decisions about Starlink were made by the US military or the president, while Trump denied responsibility and Secretary of State Marco Rubio affirmed that Ukraine’s access to Starlink remained intact.

sources.text:
US Citizen Stephen Hubbard Is Released by Russia as Donald Trump Claims There Was 'No Swap' Made
Russia has freed American teacher Stephen Hubbard after more than four years in detention, with Donald Trump saying no prisoner swap was required
Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American teacher held in Russia for more than four years, has been released and was at St Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport on Wednesday, according to President Vladimir Putin. US President Donald Trump said the release followed his direct request to Putin and insisted that Washington gave Moscow nothing in return.
Trump wrote on Truth Social that Hubbard was freed 'at the request of President Donald J. Trump, made directly to President Vladimir Putin in a telephone conversation last week'. He added that the United States was 'not required to give anything in return' and that 'there was no "swap" necessary for this release'.
The announcement came as Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff, met Putin in St Petersburg for talks centred on the war in Ukraine. Witkoff thanked the Russian president in person, telling him: 'Because of you, he's going home to his family.'
Why Trump Says No Swap Was Needed
Hubbard had been held since 2022, after Russian forces captured him in Ukraine following Moscow's full-scale invasion.
Russian authorities accused the retired Michigan schoolteacher of working as a mercenary for Ukraine, including manning a checkpoint, and sentenced him in 2024 to almost seven years in a penal colony. His family has consistently maintained his innocence.
The US State Department had formally designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained. He was, according to the source material, the last American in Russia carrying that designation, although as many as 10 other Americans, including dual nationals, remain in Russian custody.
Trump's claim of an uncomplicated humanitarian release is likely to attract scrutiny. He also linked Hubbard's freedom to his decision, five days earlier, to waive some sanctions on Russia before they were due to take effect.
In a second Truth Social post, Trump said people who had wanted the sanctions imposed had since apologised because they did not know he was negotiating Hubbard's release. He claimed that, had the sanctions gone ahead, the negotiations 'would have come to a complete and total halt'.
That is the president's account, not an independently verified explanation from the Kremlin. Putin, according to Russian state media, said Hubbard was released 'for humanitarian reasons'.
A Release With Political Timing
Witkoff arrived in St Petersburg shortly after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway, where the two discussed repairing a relationship that has been strained in recent weeks.
Following Putin's decision to free Hubbard, the Russian president had a public gesture to point to ahead of talks on Ukraine. The release also enabled Trump to highlight his use of personal diplomacy and a softer line towards Moscow.
Witkoff's comments to Putin were notably positive. He told the Russian leader: 'You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian, you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that.'
The remarks came at a time when Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of limiting intelligence sharing, slowing Starlink services and delaying weapons supplies.
Who Is Stephen Hubbard?
Hubbard spent decades abroad as an English teacher and moved to Izyum in eastern Ukraine in 2014. The city was occupied by Russian forces early in the 2022 invasion.
Russian state media reported that prosecutors alleged he signed a contract worth about $1,000 per month (€850 and £750) to fight for Ukraine. His sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, called the accusation a lie.
A retired schoolteacher, Hubbard had served in the US National Guard and Air Force. He is reported to be in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment at a military hospital.
His son, Joseph Coleman, thanked Trump and US officials for securing the release. 'Never once did we waver as we prayed for success in these negotiations,' he said, while also describing Putin's action as a 'humanitarian move' that the family deeply appreciated.
Other Americans Remain Detained
Hubbard's release follows other recent cases of Americans leaving Russian custody. Robert Gilman, a former Marine detained for more than four years, was freed in August after his health deteriorated to a life-threatening condition.
Marc Fogel was released early last year, while journalist Evan Gershkovich and Marine veteran Paul Whelan were among those freed in a multi-country prisoner exchange in 2024.
Americans including Andre Khachatoorian, David Barnes, Aleksandr Antonov, Olga Jezler and Chuck Zimmerman remain in Russian custody, according to the source material. Several deny the charges against them, and their families say US citizenship or political circumstances influenced their detention.
The State Department continues to advise Americans not to travel to Russia, warning of the risk of wrongful detention, arbitrary enforcement of local laws and limited consular assistance.
Hubbard has been released. Officials and analysts have not yet indicated whether his case could affect ongoing efforts to secure the release of other detained Americans.

sources.text:
By Dasha Litvinova and Eric Tucker
Russia on Wednesday freed an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, in a deal completed during a visit by a top U.S. envoy and at a time when President Donald Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Moscow.
Trump said in a Truth Social post that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call last week to free Stephen Hubbard, and that, unlike previous releases, his had not required the U.S. to give up anyone in return.
“Welcome home, Stephen, it’s great to have you back,” Trump said.
Trending
Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher from Michigan, was on his way home following a visit to St. Petersburg by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who also held talks with Putin about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Hubbard was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison following a closed trial. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, and that he fought alongside Kyiv’s forces until being captured two months later. The U.S. government under the Biden administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained.
The release came amid Trump moves to benefit Russia
Witkoff, a key Trump administration figure who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February 2027, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he’s going home to his family.”
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media on Wednesday that Hubbard’s release was “raised by the American side for a certain time,” and Putin decided to free the man out of “humanitarian considerations.”
He added that general contacts “continue on a regular basis between the intelligence services.”
The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin.
Those include Trump’s decision last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after the late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Moscow’s war. That reversal followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks Wednesday with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg.
Other Americans remain jailed in Russia
Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer.
Other Americans, including some with serious illnesses, remain jailed in Russia. Hubbard was the only one designated as wrongfully detained, although advocates say that label should be applied to other prisoners.
Global Reach, a group that works to free Americans detained abroad and currently represents five American held in Russia, praised the release but called for the other prisoners to come home as well.
“We are grateful to the Trump Administration for reuniting Stephen Hubbard with his family, but at the same time, we know that there are five other families of Americans held in Russia who are going to have a hard time understanding why their loved one was not included in the deal,” Eric Lebson, the group’s chief strategy officer, said in a statement.
Hubbard had been imprisoned since 2022 on charges that Hostage Aid Worldwide, a hostage advocacy group, has called bogus.
The organization in August posted an open letter to Trump that it said was written by Patricia Hubbard Fox, Hubbard’s sister, in which she offered praise for Trump but also said her brother had been subjected to “constant beatings, torture and starvation” while in custody.
“Even so, everything that you’re doing isn’t going to matter to my kidnapped, American Veteran brother, Stephen James Hubbard (soon to be 74) if Putin won’t cave and let him come home and he dies up there in a Nazi prison (crying),” the letter said.

Putin Releases American Stephen Hubbard After Four Years in Russian Prison Following Trump Appeal
sources.text:
Retired Michigan teacher Stephen Hubbard, 74, is returning to the United States following a personal request from President Donald Trump to Russian President Vladimir Putin, with Moscow granting his release during renewed diplomatic negotiations over the war in Ukraine.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
An American citizen imprisoned in Russia since the opening months of the Ukraine war was freed Wednesday, Oct. 21, after President Donald Trump personally intervened with Russian President Vladimir Putin, bringing an end to more than four years of detention without a prisoner exchange.
Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan, was released as U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff arrived in St. Petersburg for high-level negotiations with Putin concerning the war in Ukraine. Russian officials described the decision as a humanitarian gesture, while Trump announced that Washington had not been required to release a Russian prisoner or provide another concession in exchange for Hubbard’s freedom.
“Welcome home, Stephen, it’s great to have you back,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social message celebrating the release.
Putin announced the decision during his meeting with Witkoff, informing the American envoy that Hubbard had already been transferred to St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport. The release followed a telephone conversation between Trump and Putin the previous week, during which the American president raised Hubbard’s case and requested that he be allowed to return home.
According to Reuters, Hubbard had been held by Russian authorities since April 2022 after being captured in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izium. Russian prosecutors accused him of working with Ukrainian military forces against Russia, allegations disputed by his family and American legal representatives.
Hubbard’s departure marks the second release of an American detainee from Russian custody in approximately two months. It also represents a diplomatic development for the Trump administration as Washington attempts to restart negotiations aimed at ending a conflict that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Witkoff thanked Putin during their meeting and credited the Russian leader with authorizing Hubbard’s return to his family.
“Because of you, he’s going home to his family,” Witkoff said.
The American envoy went further in his remarks, acknowledging Putin’s decision as an act of humanitarian consideration.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov subsequently confirmed that Hubbard’s detention had been discussed between Russian and American representatives for an extended period. He said Putin had decided to grant the release based on “humanitarian considerations,” including the prisoner’s circumstances.
Peskov said the matter had been “raised by the American side for a certain time,” indicating that the decision followed previous contacts rather than arising solely from Wednesday’s meeting.
The spokesman also acknowledged continuing communication between the two countries’ security agencies.
General contacts “continue on a regular basis between the intelligence services,” Peskov said.
Hubbard’s release concludes a detention that began amid the rapid Russian military advance into eastern Ukraine during the first months of the invasion. The retired American teacher had been living in Ukraine when Russian troops captured him in April 2022.
Moscow accused Hubbard of signing a contract with Ukrainian military forces and participating in territorial defense operations against Russian troops. Prosecutors alleged that he had served at a Ukrainian checkpoint near Izium, where Russian forces took him into custody.
His case eventually proceeded through the Russian court system, culminating in a closed-door trial in 2024. Hubbard was convicted of mercenary activity and sentenced to six years and 10 months in prison.
Russian state media reported that Hubbard had admitted guilt, but his American attorney, Martin De Luca, disputed the government’s characterization of the case. De Luca said his client denied participating in military operations or joining a Ukrainian combat unit.
Hubbard’s family also maintained that the allegations were false and repeatedly sought assistance from American authorities to secure his release.
The Biden administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained, a classification used by the U.S. government when officials determine that an American’s imprisonment abroad meets established criteria for diplomatic intervention.
The designation placed his case within a specialized federal process for seeking the return of Americans whose detention is considered improper. At the time of Wednesday’s release, Hubbard was the only American remaining in Russian custody who carried that official designation.
His relatives and advocates had long expressed concerns about his age, health and treatment in prison, warning that continued detention could jeopardize his life.
Those concerns became particularly urgent during the summer, when relatives appealed publicly to the Trump administration for stronger intervention.
In August, Hostage Aid Worldwide, an organization advocating for Americans detained overseas, published an open letter attributed to Hubbard’s sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox. The letter described serious concerns about his treatment in Russian custody and urged Trump to secure his freedom before his condition deteriorated further.
Fox alleged that her brother had endured “constant beatings, torture and starvation” while imprisoned. Those allegations could not be independently verified, but they illustrated the fears his family had repeatedly communicated to American officials.
“Even so, everything that you’re doing isn’t going to matter to my kidnapped, American Veteran brother, Stephen James Hubbard (soon to be 74) if Putin won’t cave and let him come home and he dies up there in a Nazi prison (crying),” the letter stated.
The family maintained that Hubbard had been unjustly imprisoned and required urgent assistance because of his age and deteriorating health.
Wednesday’s announcement brought relief to supporters who had spent years urging successive American administrations to negotiate his return.
The release occurred during a period of renewed diplomatic activity involving Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, with the Trump administration pressing both sides to consider proposals intended to end the war before its fifth anniversary in February 2027.
Before traveling to Russia, Witkoff met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo, Norway, on Tuesday, Oct. 20. The discussions included representatives of European governments and focused on potential arrangements for ending the fighting and establishing security guarantees.
The American envoy traveled to St. Petersburg carrying proposals developed through those consultations, with the goal of determining whether Moscow would agree to resume direct negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States.
According to Axios reporting on Wednesday’s talks, Witkoff presented Putin with an updated diplomatic framework and requested the resumption of three-party negotiations. The Kremlin subsequently indicated that Putin had agreed in principle to renewed talks after Nov. 10, although substantial disagreements remained over territory and security arrangements.
The discussions took place against a backdrop of continuing Russian military operations in Ukraine and growing disagreements between Washington and Kyiv over the terms of a possible settlement.
Trump has repeatedly pushed Ukrainian officials to accept compromises that he argues are necessary to end the conflict. Zelenskyy has maintained that any agreement must address Ukraine’s security and sovereignty while preventing further Russian attacks.
The diplomatic developments have also coincided with significant changes in American economic policy toward Moscow.
Last week, Trump waived sanctions imposed under legislation that Congress had approved with overwhelming bipartisan support to increase financial pressure on Russia. The measure, associated with the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, sought to restrict revenue streams supporting Moscow’s military operations.
The decision to suspend those sanctions was accompanied by an announcement that the United States would begin importing Russian diesel fuel as part of an effort to reduce domestic energy prices.
The administration has promoted the arrangement as a potential means of easing fuel costs before the November congressional elections. However, the extent to which Russian diesel imports could influence American gasoline and diesel prices remains uncertain.
The policy changes have prompted questions about whether Washington is reducing economic pressure on Moscow while seeking concessions in peace negotiations.
Trump has maintained that his diplomatic strategy is intended to produce a negotiated end to the war. His administration has also pointed to the release of detained Americans as evidence that direct engagement with Putin can deliver results.
The decision to free Hubbard without an announced prisoner exchange distinguishes his case from previous arrangements in which Russia released Americans in return for Russian nationals held by Western governments.
In August, Russia freed former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman, who had been imprisoned following disputed allegations that he assaulted a police officer. Gilman had experienced serious health problems during his detention.
Other Americans have also returned from Russian custody through diplomatic negotiations and prisoner exchanges. Former teacher Marc Fogel was released in February 2025 after spending more than three years in Russian custody following a drug-related conviction.
Despite those releases, several Americans remain imprisoned in Russia, including individuals whose families and legal representatives dispute the allegations against them.
The advocacy organization Global Reach, which works to secure the freedom of Americans detained abroad, welcomed Hubbard’s release but emphasized that the government must continue pursuing the return of other prisoners.
The organization said it currently represents five Americans held in Russia and expressed concern that families whose relatives remain incarcerated would struggle with the news that another prisoner had been freed while their own cases remained unresolved.
“We are grateful to the Trump Administration for reuniting Stephen Hubbard with his family, but at the same time, we know that there are five other families of Americans held in Russia who are going to have a hard time understanding why their loved one was not included in the deal,” Eric Lebson, Global Reach’s chief strategy officer, said in a statement.
Advocates have called for broader use of the U.S. government’s wrongful detention designation, arguing that additional American prisoners meet the criteria for diplomatic intervention.
The classification can affect the resources and diplomatic attention devoted to a detention case, but Americans who do not receive it may still receive consular assistance and other forms of government support.
Hubbard’s release was welcomed across organizations that had followed his case, particularly because of concerns about his medical condition and the length of his imprisonment.
For his family, the decision ends more than four years of uncertainty surrounding his confinement following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
For Washington and Moscow, the release demonstrates that limited humanitarian agreements remain possible even as the two countries continue negotiating over the much broader military and geopolitical issues surrounding the conflict.
Whether Wednesday’s meeting produces progress toward ending the war remains uncertain. Russia and Ukraine continue to disagree over territorial control, security guarantees and the conditions under which hostilities might cease.
Putin’s decision to free Hubbard, however, provided an immediate outcome from the latest diplomatic contacts and allowed an American previously designated as wrongfully detained to begin his journey home.
The Associated Press reported that the release was completed while Witkoff was meeting Russian leaders in St. Petersburg, with American officials confirming that the retired teacher was no longer in Russian custody.
Hubbard is now returning to the United States after more than four years of imprisonment, while negotiations over the Ukraine war and efforts to free other detained Americans continue.

Trump asks Putin to free jailed US citizen, Russia releases him ahead of envoy visit
Stephen Hubbard, who was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison in 2024, was freed on humanitarian grounds after Trump's direct appeal to Russia's Putin.
Russia has released 74-year-old American citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine, ahead of US special envoy Steve Witkoff's meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday.
The release came as Washington stepped up efforts to revive peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine amid growing strains in US-Kyiv relations.
US President Donald Trump announced Hubbard's release on social media, saying it followed a request he had made directly to Putin during a phone conversation last week. Hubbard, a retired teacher from Michigan, had been designated by the US State Department as wrongfully detained.
"Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family," Trump said, adding that no prisoner exchange was required to secure his release.
Russian state media reported that Putin had ordered Hubbard's release on humanitarian grounds. During his meeting with Witkoff at the Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, Putin said Hubbard had been taken to Pulkovo Airport, the same airport where the US envoy had landed earlier that day.
The release was the first major development announced during Witkoff's visit and was presented as a goodwill gesture ahead of discussions on restarting US-mediated peace talks. Trump also suggested that his administration's recent decision to ease certain Russian sanctions had helped create the conditions for negotiations, saying that without the move, the talks would have come to a halt.
Hubbard's son, Joseph Coleman, thanked Trump and other US officials for securing his father’s release, while Witkoff conveyed the American president's gratitude directly to Putin.
WHO IS STEPHEN HUBBARD?
Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher who spent decades working abroad as an English teacher, moved to the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum in 2014.
Russian prosecutors alleged that Hubbard joined a Ukrainian military defence unit in Izyum after signing a contract that paid him approximately USD 1,000 a month. Russian forces captured him shortly after launching their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
He was subsequently charged with serving as a mercenary and sentenced in October 2024 to nearly seven years in a penal colony. During a court hearing in October 2024, Hubbard appeared in a glass enclosure at the Moscow City Court.
The US State Department later designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained, a classification used by the American government in cases where it believes a US citizen has been unjustly held abroad.
According to CBS News, Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for medical treatment.
TRUMP, WITKOFF THANK PUTIN FOR RELEASE
Announcing the development on Wednesday, Trump said Hubbard had been released at his request and that Russia had not sought anything in return.
The US president also linked the outcome to his administration's recent decision to ease certain Russian sanctions. He said that had he not taken the step, negotiations would have come to a "complete and total halt".
Hubbard's son, Joseph Coleman, expressed gratitude to the US administration and Russian leadership for the outcome.
"Never once did we waver as we prayed for success in these negotiations, and we must acknowledge that this humanitarian move by President Putin in this matter is deeply appreciated," Coleman said.
Witkoff also personally thanked Putin during their meeting, conveying the gratitude of Trump and the American public.
"I want to thank you very much, the President sends his thanks the whole nation sends their thanks because of Stephen Hubbard. Because of you, he's going home to his family," Witkoff said, according to remarks carried by Russian state media.
WITKOFF URGES PUTIN TO RESUME PEACE TALKS
Witkoff’s visit to St Petersburg followed talks in Oslo on Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, alongside European and NATO representatives.
The Oslo discussions sought to coordinate positions on a possible peace framework before Witkoff’s meeting with Putin. A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Ukraine had presented new ideas and proposals that had helped make meaningful progress towards a coordinated approach to engaging with Russia.
The talks covered key elements of a potential comprehensive settlement, including security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and a broader European security architecture, the official said.
Witkoff told Putin that one of his objectives was to explore whether trilateral negotiations involving the United States, Russia and Ukraine could resume.
"One thing that I hope to accomplish today is to have some good conversation between us about the resumption potentially of trilateral talks between Ukraine and Russia and the United States," he said.
"Even if we don't have a resolution today, if we just talk about and sort of consider what that next step might be, I think that would be important and the world is waiting to hear that," he added.
The latest diplomatic effort comes more than two years after Trump promised during his election campaign to end the war within 24 hours. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February, before the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran.
Despite renewed engagement, Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart on the terms of a possible settlement. Putin has continued to seek full Russian control over the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and has opposed Ukraine joining NATO. The Kremlin has also said that any meeting between Putin and Zelensky would require extensive preparation by aides to ensure it could produce meaningful results.
Zelensky has expressed hope for a trilateral meeting involving himself, Putin and Trump to discuss the central issues preventing a settlement. Trump, meanwhile, has intensified pressure on Kyiv to reach an agreement, warning on Tuesday that Ukraine needed to end the war or face "a very bad thing".

Trump Admits He Made Huge Concession to Free American in Russia
Donald Trump claimed he hadn’t given up anything to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard from Russian prison—and then immediately admitted he actually had.
Samuel Corum/Sipa/Bloomberg/Getty Images
Moments after declaring that the U.S. “gave nothing” to Russia in exchange for the release of imprisoned American Stephen Hubbard, Donald Trump revealed that we did, in fact, give something.
“So we appreciate the fact that we were able to get him. We gave nothing in exchange, which is very rare. We never give anything in exchange,” said Trump during a roundtable at the White House Wednesday.
But just moments later, Trump seemed to refer to bipartisan blowback he had faced earlier this month for striking a diesel deal with Russia and dropping America’s economic sanctions against the global superpower.
“I was in the midst of getting Stephen out of Russia and, if we did what these foolish people wanted me to do, he wouldn’t be coming out right now. He’d be in there for another 20 years,” Trump said. “So the last thing I was going to do was break up that.”
Hubbard, a retired American teacher, had lived in Ukraine for years before he was captured by Russia in the early weeks of the war. Two years later in 2024, he was convicted by a Russian court of serving as a mercenary. Hubbard was released early Wednesday after nearly five cumulative years in detention.
The 74-year-old Michigander’s release was followed by a jarringly obsequious meeting between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin, during which Witkoff referred to the notoriously tyrannical Russian leader as a “humanitarian.”
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Witkoff told Putin Wednesday, responding to Hubbard’s release. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again.”
Even Republicans had a hard time standing by the Trump envoy’s messaging. Reacting to a video of the exchange on X, North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis slammed Witkoff’s descriptor as an “embarrassing and outrageous thing to say.”
“You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian,’” Tillis wrote.
Senator John Cornyn of Texas commented that Putin is a “stone cold killer.”
But Trump wasn’t willing to join the choir. When asked to respond to Witkoff’s exchange, Trump told reporters that he didn’t want to “upset an apple cart where we’re getting close to settling a war.”
Trump Falls Asleep on Camera Again (He Also Fell Asleep Yesterday)

President Donald Trump falls asleep as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during a roundtable in the White House on October 21.

President Donald Trump falls asleep as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during a roundtable in the White House on October 21.
Our 80-year-old president is once again struggling to stay awake on camera.

The crowd quickly erupted in chants of “USA! USA!”

“If Greg Landsman had his way, he would take our country right back to where we were four years ago,” Vance said of Conroy’s Democratic opponent. “He would raise your taxes, he would bring us back to the highest inflation in 40 years. He would invite—”
“You protected pedophiles!” a young man in a suit and a MAGA hat right behind Vance shouted. He threw the hat to the ground as the crowd began to drown him out with boos and that classic “USA” chant. He was quickly removed from the rally.

Because when he took that hat off it was very obvious that he has not washed his hair in about three months,” Vance joked, to mild applause. “And we all know that the people who haven’t washed their hair in three months, they vote for Democrats, not Republicans.”

What an odd response to someone for bringing up perhaps one of the biggest failures of Donald Trump’s second term: the botched, obscured, and incomplete rollout of the Epstein files. And does Vance really want to argue that MAGA supporters are across the board more hygienic than Democrats?

Todd Blanche Says Everyone Else Is Confused About DOJ Independence
Apparently, it’s supposed to run according to the president’s whims.
Tom Brenner/The Washington Post/Bloomberg/Getty Images
Attorney General Todd Blanche’s understanding of the Justice Department is a stark departure from the law enforcement agency’s historic position within the federal government.
Speaking with the New York Post podcast Wednesday, Blanche boldly declared that he works “for President Trump.”
“There was this misperception that there’s this separation and independence between the Department of Justice and the White House, and everybody likes to champion that, and they accused me of not suffering from independence,” Blanche said. “I don’t.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche says there's a "misperception that there's this separation and independence between the Department of Justice and the White House."
"I work for President Trump."
Contrary to Blanche’s opinion, the Justice Department is supposed to be independent and free from presidential interference. That’s been true since at least Watergate, after which the agency established interdepartmental policies and new political norms to distance its operations from the White House.
But that started to shift in 2024, when the Supreme Court sided with Donald Trump to expand his presidential immunity. At the time, Chief Justice John Roberts penned a majority decision that effectively transformed the Justice Department into an arm to be leveraged by the Oval Office, opening communication channels between the federal law enforcement agency and the presidency for all future investigations.
“The president may discuss potential investigations and prosecutions with his Attorney General and other Justice Department officials to carry out his constitutional duty to ‘take care that the laws be faithfully executed,’” Roberts wrote in his majority opinion.

Zelensky said the meeting was productive and expressed his openness to a "potential trilateral meeting of the leaders to address the issues that only the leaders can do." However, he emphasized that any meetings to negotiate an end to the war must include Ukrainian officials, insisting there should be “nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine."
Zelensky's remarks came after the Wall Street Journal reported that Putin had floated the idea of a summit with Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to discuss a potential Ukraine deal. Trump on Monday said he was open to a trilateral summit with those attendees to discuss matters related to “denuclearization.”
U.S.-Ukraine tensions escalate
Ukraine and U.S. officials remain at odds as to why Kyiv has experienced limited access to Starshield, the military-grade counterpart of SpaceX’s Starlink commercial service. The program, which offers remote Internet connectivity from satellites in low-Earth orbit, has become a lifeline for Ukraine on the battlefield, allowing it to execute long-reach drone strike missions and counter attacks.
On Oct. 14, Ukraine said its access to Starshield was abruptly limited. Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelensky, said speed restrictions had been imposed, leading to the “failure” of several military missions. Beskrestnov claimed the restrictions, which he said applied to devices traveling over 100 miles per hour and using Starshield, were “related to the current political situation.” During an Oct. 18 appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Zelensky said he believed the limited Starshield speed was a “message” from the U.S. government. He also said that Washington had briefly stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, drawing a denial from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Zelensky’s remarks came after Reuters reported, citing two U.S. officials, that an order to limit Starshield services in Ukraine had come from inside the White House. When approached for comment, a senior U.S. official told TIME: “No such request was ever made by the President.” Some Republican lawmakers, including Representative Mike Turner of Ohio and Senator Kevin Cramer of North Dakota, have joined bipartisan calls for an investigation to determine the cause.
Addressing the matter, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS.”

President Donald Trump's designated special envoy, Steve Witkoff, travelled to Russia on Wednesday to engage in discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin and facilitate the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired educator from Michigan who had remained in Russian custody since 2022, as reported by Russian state-controlled media outlets.
Witkoff meets Putin
Witkoff arrived in the Russian city of St. Petersburg on Wednesday morning, a confirmation provided by a Kremlin spokesperson, in preparation for the scheduled engagement with Putin.
Trump's envoy expressed gratitude to Putin for the release of Hubbard, according to an official statement regarding the meeting disseminated by Russia's state-controlled RIA Novosti news organization. Putin said that Hubbard, who had been apprehended in eastern Ukraine in April 2022, was transported to St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport, the statement noted.
A spokesperson from the Kremlin, Yuri Ushakov, informed members of the press on Wednesday that Witkoff was scheduled to hold discussions with Putin at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg during the morning hours, according to statements carried by Russian state media outlets.

The negotiations focused on Hubbard and numerous other American nationals imprisoned by the Russian government on charges that the administration contends are without legitimate foundation, ABC News reported, citing a source.

Hubbard obtained a master's degree in English literature and spent approximately 25 years residing in Japan, where he worked as an English instructor. sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Russia did not ask for anything in return for the release of an American prisoner on Wednesday, which was announced at a meeting between President Vladimir Putin and U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff. However, he later appeared to say it was linked to sanctions on Russia.
Putin said on Wednesday that Russia had released Stephen Hubbard, 74, a retired teacher from Michigan, who had been jailed for six years and 10 months in 2024 for allegedly fighting for Ukraine. Putin said that Hubbard had been taken to an airport in St. Petersburg.
Following the announcement, Trump posted on Truth Social that he had asked for Hubbard to be released during a call with Putin last week.
"The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return—an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no 'swap' necessary for this release," Trump said.
However, Trump appeared to contradict this in a follow-up post in which he said that the release of Hubbard was in fact tied to sanctions on Russia.
"Numerous people, who requested that sanctions be immediately imposed on Russia, have called to apologize to President Trump in that they didn’t know that he was negotiating the release of Stephen Hubbard," wrote Trump.
"If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt," he added.
Trump later appeared to acknowledge that his decision not to impose sanctions on Russia was linked to the negotiations for Hubbard’s release, despite insisting that the United States gave nothing in return.
“We were in the midst of negotiating and a lot of... stupid people said why aren’t you putting Russian sanctions - in the midst of negotiations to get a longtime hostage back from Russia."” Trump told reporters outside the White House.
"But you said you didn’t give anything for his release?" CNN’s Kaitlan Collins asked.
”If I didn’t do that, you wouldn’t have him coming back," Trump responded, before personally attacking Collins, telling her, “You don’t know anything.... You don’t know what you’re talking about. You’re a low IQ person. You’re a dummy.”
Last year, the Trump administration secured the release of another American jailed in Russia, schoolteacher Marc Fogel, who had been jailed for 14 years following a drug smuggling conviction.
Ukraine and its allies have condemned the Trump administration's easing of sanctions on Russian diesel in a deal announced last week with the aim of curbing gas prices for Americans.
What Was Said at the Meeting Between Putin and Witkoff?
Witkoff thanked Putin for the diesel deal on Wednesday, saying: "I think that was a really important act on your part, sir."
"I know the president is deeply grateful for it, as are our farmers and truckers who use diesel and have been adversely affected by this diesel crisis," Witkoff said. "It's an example of us all working together, and I want to say thank you to you for that."
Witkoff also said there was "a foundation in place to move toward a ceasefire" in the Russia-Ukraine war following "constructive" discussions with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway the previous day.
The U.S. envoy also asked Putin to consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S., something which the Russian president has long avoided.
Putin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the partially occupied Donbas, which for Ukraine, would be an unacceptable concession.
Zelensky Calls For Ceasefire
Following Witkoff's meeting, Zelensky again rejected the prospect that Ukraine would hand over its eastern Donbas region to end the war in an interview with Fox News.
He told anchor Brian Kilmeade that despite Putin's claims, Moscow is not winning on the ground and is using massive drone and missile attacks on civilians to force land concessions they haven't earned.
The Ukrainian president proposed an immediate ceasefire where troops currently stand ahead of peace talks for a long-term solution.
"We stay strong. People are tired of course. We want to end this war as quick as possible," Zelensky said. "I think we have to start from the point where we stay, move to a diplomatic way, and then on the tactical level, we will find a way of peace plan and resettlement."
