sources.news_title: Putin Frees U.S. Teacher as Witkoff Brings Peace Plan
sources.text:
Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired schoolteacher from Michigan held since April 2022, on Wednesday as President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff sat down with Vladimir Putin at the Constantine Palace outside St. Petersburg to present an updated American proposal for ending the war in Ukraine. The release, confirmed in a Kremlin readout carried by the RIA Novosti state agency, came less than 24 hours after Witkoff left Oslo, where a U.S. official described talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders as "constructive" and said the parties had reached "strong alignment at the working level."
Putin told Witkoff during the meeting that Hubbard had already been taken to Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg, and Witkoff thanked the Russian leader for the release, according to the readout. Two U.S. officials and a third source told ABC News before the meeting that the administration was closing in on a broader deal that would free multiple Americans held in Russia on charges Washington regards as dubious, with Hubbard at the center of the talks. Whether others were released alongside him was not immediately clear.
Hubbard had lived as a civilian in eastern Ukraine since around 2014, teaching English, according to his family. Russian forces detained him in the Kharkiv region town of Izium in the opening weeks of the full-scale invasion and later charged him with fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine, a charge his family and the State Department said was false. A Moscow court sentenced him in October 2024 to nearly seven years in prison; the State Department subsequently designated him wrongfully detained, the formal status that opens the way to negotiated release.
Trump had telegraphed the outcome on Tuesday. Asked in the Oval Office whether a deal to free Hubbard was imminent, the president declined to confirm it but said he had discussed the case with Putin "at length" and had "asked him to release him." "Let's see what happens," Trump said. "I'd love to get him back."
The prisoner release gave Putin a low-cost gesture to offer at the start of a meeting the Kremlin had framed in advance as being about Ukraine. Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian reporters on Wednesday morning that Putin would receive Witkoff "in the first half of the day" at the Constantine Palace in Strelna, that Ukraine would dominate the agenda, and that Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's investment envoy who has become the Kremlin's main back-channel to the Trump team, would also attend. Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and co-negotiator, joined by video after illness kept him from traveling to Oslo and then to Russia. Ushakov said "I don't know whether any agreement will be reached today," and that Moscow had had "no contact with Zelensky" in the recent talks. He added that Putin and Trump could meet on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China next month, as both leaders were interested in attending.
What Witkoff carried to Strelna was the product of the Oslo session. The U.S. official who briefed reporters after Tuesday's talks said Ukraine had "brought forward new ideas and proposals, which were discussed in detail," and that the discussion covered "key elements of a comprehensive peace framework," including security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and a broader European security architecture. The aim of the St. Petersburg meeting, the official said, was to "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations."
That last phrase is where the two sides' positions diverge most sharply. Zelensky said in Oslo that the next step should be a meeting between himself, Putin and Trump, a format Moscow has rejected throughout the year of shuttle diplomacy. Putin has met Witkoff repeatedly, including a three-hour Kremlin session with Witkoff and Kushner on Sept. 5, and has sent Dmitriev to Washington and Miami, but he has not agreed to sit across a table from Zelensky, whom the Kremlin continues to describe as lacking legitimacy. Russian officials said after the September round that Moscow's position on territory and Ukraine's future alignment was unchanged.
The Oslo meeting itself was a larger affair than the bilateral it was first billed as. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb hosted, and representatives from France, Britain, Germany, Poland, the European Union and NATO took part, according to Axios. Zelensky presented Witkoff with a Ukrainian state award at the Norwegian government's official residence before the talks began, footage posted by the Ukrainian president showed.
Witkoff plans to return to Oslo for further consultations after the Russia leg, Støre told broadcaster NRK on Wednesday. "I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," he said.
Zelensky emerged with one concrete gain. He told a news conference after the meeting, and after an earlier phone call with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, that Ukraine was again receiving American early warning of Russian missile launches. "Now it works, it's great," he said. Kyiv had complained for more than a week that the warning feed, along with access to the Starshield military satellite service, had been curtailed as Washington pressed Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries. Zelensky said he and Rubio had also discussed Patriot interceptor supplies and the Starlink system, which Ukrainian units said had stopped working when mounted on fast-moving platforms such as drones.
He also said he had discussed "Article 5-like" security guarantees, a reference to NATO's collective defense clause, and that the American side had "underlined again that it will be strong." Stubb told the same news conference that "the process is back on track," and Støre called the day good and constructive. Zelensky said separately that Ukraine was prepared to cease strikes on Russian refineries if Moscow took reciprocal steps, a conditional version of the 30-day pause he offered U.S. senators the previous day.
The refinery question was the sharpest point of friction inside the room. Kushner, joining by video, "was very direct" in pressing Trump's demand that Ukraine halt the refinery campaign, according to a person with knowledge of the discussion cited by Axios. Ukraine had paused the strikes for several days in deference to Trump's request earlier this month, then resumed them after Russia showed no sign of observing the energy ceasefire Trump had announced, and last weekend sent roughly 1,000 drones at targets including a St. Petersburg oil terminal.
Trump's own comments on Tuesday placed the burden of settlement squarely on Kyiv. "Ukraine has to want to settle this war," he told reporters, adding that he believed Moscow wanted to get it done. "If they don't make a deal, it's just gonna get worse" for Ukraine, he said. "We want Zelensky to make a deal." He suggested Russia held the upper hand on the battlefield: "Russia is a big machine — they just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done. They've taken a very large piece of land."
He returned to the theme of American generosity unrewarded. "We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We've got nothing back other than high diesel," Trump said, in a reference to the fuel-price argument the administration has used to justify lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. "We have given, probably, possibly, more money to Ukraine than almost anybody over the years, hundreds of billions of dollars. We've got nothing back, and the American taxpayers are tired of it."
The remarks capped ten days in which Washington's relationship with Kyiv sank to what the Associated Press called a new low. The sequence began with the diesel deal agreed directly between Trump and Putin, continued with Trump's weekend waiver of the Graham Act sanctions he had signed into law, and ran through reports that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had not signed off on a batch of Patriot interceptors that European allies had already bought and paid for under the NATO-run PURL mechanism. Trump has in the same period suggested Zelensky should be replaced.
On the Patriot question, Tuesday brought acknowledgment rather than resolution. A source familiar with the matter told Reuters that most weapons deliveries under PURL continued to flow but that Hegseth had not approved Ukraine's latest requests for Patriot interceptors. Rubio, speaking in India, conceded that a consignment of interceptors purchased by European countries for Ukraine "may not have been delivered" but denied any change in policy. "There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said.
Hegseth, asked directly about the reports, said the Pentagon had not changed its posture toward Ukraine and then explained the hold in terms of American stockpiles. "We haven't changed our posture in any way toward the Ukrainians, but certainly with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well," he said. He added that Zelensky "knows that we've had very earnest conversations with him about it" and endorsed Rubio's framing.
Zelensky's account is more specific. He has said the United States is now supplying roughly 12 Patriot interceptors a month, about a quarter of the rate under the Biden administration, and that European governments prepared to transfer interceptors from their own stockpiles are waiting on the same Pentagon signature. "Hegseth has the contracts for Patriot missiles on his desk," a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent last week. Zelensky told senators on Monday that Ukraine had "almost no Patriot interceptors left" from the U.S. batch.
Hegseth also addressed Starlink, saying Washington had not pulled back Ukraine's ability to access the SpaceX network and suggesting the problem lay with corporate terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with. That account sits awkwardly with Tuesday's Wall Street Journal report, citing U.S. officials, that Elon Musk ordered the slowdown after consulting Trump and other administration officials, and with an earlier Reuters report that the order came from the White House. Musk has said Starshield, the military variant, is controlled by the U.S. government and that any limits on its use are ultimately Trump's call.
Russian strikes killed four people across Ukraine overnight into Wednesday, the prime minister said, as forces bombarded cities in the west and knocked out power in regions that had largely been spared until now; energy facilities were hit in seven regions. The Lviv region was struck again during the day. In Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Russian drones hit an energy facility on Tuesday, leaving four districts without power. Russia's defense ministry said its forces struck three cargo vessels in the Danube port of Reni, two more en route to Odesa, and two logistics hubs.
The strikes came despite Trump's call earlier this month for both sides to spare each other's energy systems, a call Russia answered by hitting a Kharkiv power plant within hours and the Kyiv region's main thermal plant days later. Trump has repeatedly condemned Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries while saying little about the far heavier Russian campaign against Ukrainian power generation, a pattern European officials have noted with alarm as winter approaches.
The shape of the exchange now on the table is therefore uneven. Moscow has received, in sequence, the diesel sanctions relief, the Graham Act waiver, a pause in Ukrainian refinery strikes, and continued pressure on Kyiv to make that pause permanent; it has given back a wrongfully detained American and, according to the White House, a willingness to receive an updated proposal. Kyiv has received the restoration of missile early warning and a renewed American assurance on security guarantees; it has not received the Patriots it has already paid for or a Russian commitment to any reciprocal halt.
That asymmetry explains why Zelensky's trilateral demand matters. A framework negotiated through Witkoff's shuttle between Oslo and St. Petersburg leaves Washington as the only party talking to both sides, and leaves Ukraine dependent on American readouts of what Putin has or has not accepted. A three-way leaders' meeting would put Russian positions on the record in front of Ukraine and its European backers. Moscow's resistance to the format, and the Kremlin's insistence on Wednesday that Ukraine would "dominate" a meeting at which Ukraine was not present, are two sides of the same coin.
The domestic clock is also running. The midterm elections are 13 days away, and the diesel deal, the sanctions waiver and the Patriot hold have each drawn bipartisan criticism in Congress, from a six-senator letter demanding the diesel plan be reversed to Senator Thom Tillis calling the waiver irresponsible. A prisoner release is the kind of tangible result the White House can point to before Nov. 3; a signed framework with Russia would be a larger one, and Trump's comments on Tuesday suggest he expects Ukraine, not Russia, to supply the concessions that would make it possible.
What Putin said in Strelna beyond the Hubbard exchange had not been disclosed by Wednesday evening Moscow time; Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had cautioned in advance against expecting a "breakthrough." Previous Witkoff meetings have run three to four hours and ended with Kremlin statements describing them as useful and substantive without detailing Russia's response. If the pattern holds, the first real signal of whether the Oslo framework has traction will come not from Moscow but from whether Witkoff's next stop is Kyiv or Washington, and from whether Hegseth's signature appears on the Patriot contracts in the days that follow.

Witkoff, a key Trump administration figure who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February 2027, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he’s going home to his family.”

He later moved to Ukraine to be with a woman he had met, his lawyers said, remaining in the country after the relationship ended and living there at the time of Russia’s 2022 invasion.
His case was taken up by lawyers at the U.S.-based law firm of Boies Schiller Flexner and the Russian firm of EPAM Law, which together had represented Marc Fogel, the American teacher freed from Russian custody last year, and worked for his release.
“They thought they weren’t going to see him again alive, and Stephen didn’t think he was going to come out of there alive,” Martin De Luca, one of Hubbard’s lawyers at the Boies Schiller firm, said in an interview about Hubbard’s family. “Obviously, they’re overjoyed, but they feel very much like it’s a miracle.”
His sister said she had spoken with Hubbard after his release. “He was just laughing. He said, ‘I can’t believe this is happening,’” Hubbard Fox said of her brother.

The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin.
Those include Trump’s move last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine.
Named after the late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Moscow’s war. That decision followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg.
Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer.
Other Americans, including some with serious illnesses, remain jailed in Russia. Hubbard was the last remaining American designated as wrongfully detained, although advocates say that label should be applied to other prisoners.
Russia reported more arrests of foreigners in recent days. The FSB security service said Wednesday it detained a German national suspected of mercenary activities and last week announced arrests of a Swedish national suspected of sabotage and a Japanese journalist accused of espionage.

sources.text:

U.S. envoy calls Putin a ‘humanitarian’
Witkoff, a key Trump administration figure who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February, 2027, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he’s going home to his family.”
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media on Wednesday that Hubbard’s release was “raised by the American side for a certain time,” and Putin decided to free the man out of “humanitarian considerations.”
He added that general contacts “continue on a regular basis between the intelligence services.”
Speaking to reporters after the talks, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said the Kremlin leader had pardoned Hubbard, who upon his release was taken to the St. Petersburg airport, Pulkovo, for Witkoff to bring him home to the United States.
Video showed Witkoff and Hubbard shaking hands, with the newly released American thanking the envoy.
Witkoff introduced Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev to Hubbard and described him as someone “who had a lot to do with this happening.”
“We just met President Putin, he sends you blessings and wishes you good things,” Witkoff added.
The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin.
Those include Trump’s move last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after the late South Carolina Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fuelling Moscow’s war. That decision followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks Wednesday with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg.
Other Americans remain jailed in Russia
Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer.
Other Americans, including some with serious illnesses, remain jailed in Russia. Hubbard was the last remaining American designated as wrongfully detained, although advocates say that label should be applied to other prisoners.
Global Reach, an advocacy group that works to free Americans detained abroad and currently represents five Americans held in Russia, praised the release but called for the other prisoners to come home as well.
“We are grateful to the Trump Administration for reuniting Stephen Hubbard with his family, but at the same time, we know that there are five other families of Americans held in Russia who are going to have a hard time understanding why their loved one was not included in the deal,” Eric Lebson, the group’s chief strategy officer, said in a statement.
Hubbard had been imprisoned since 2022 on charges that Hostage Aid Worldwide, a hostage advocacy group, has called bogus.
The organization earlier this year posted a letter to Trump that it said was written by Patricia Hubbard Fox, Hubbard’s sister, in which she offered praise for Trump but also said her brother had been subjected to “constant beatings, torture and starvation” while in custody.
“Even so, everything that you’re doing isn’t going to matter to my kidnapped, American Veteran brother, Stephen James Hubbard (soon to be 74) if Putin won’t cave and let him come home and he dies up there in a Nazi prison (crying),” the letter said.
Russia reported more arrests of foreigners in recent days. The FSB security service said Wednesday it detained a German national suspected of mercenary activities and last week announced arrests of a Swedish national suspected of sabotage and a Japanese journalist accused of espionage.

Russia frees retired US teacher jailed for four years after being captured in Ukraine

Russian president Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday that Moscow has agreed to free the imprisoned US citizen Stephen Hubbard following a plea from US president Donald Trump.
Mr Hubbard, 74, had been held in Russian custody since April 2022 and was serving a nearly seven-year prison sentence in a penal colony for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, charges he denies.
Putin told US special envoy Steve Witkoff that the former schoolteacher was at the St Petersburg Pulkovo airport and waiting to fly back to the US with him. Witkoff thanked him for the goodwill gesture.
The US envoy flew into Russia's second city on Wednesday morning to review new ideas on ending the war in Europe, with allies anxious that president Trump appears to be turning away from Kyiv while firming up relations with Moscow.
President Trump welcomed the news of Hubbard’s release on Wednesday, claiming the retired schoolteacher was released at his request in a telephone call with Putin last week.
“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return - an unprecedented situation for Russia,” the president said.
“There was no “swap” necessary for this release. This major return should have taken place long ago through the Biden Administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin.”
Following a closed trial, a Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary in October 2024 and sentenced him to six years and 10 months in prison.
Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised $1,000 a month. Russian state media said he had pleaded guilty to the charges he faced.
Family questioned the reported confession, however, saying Hubbard held pro-Russian views and was unlikely to have taken up arms in his seventies.
Martin De Luca, his US-based lawyer, told Reuters in June 2025 that Hubbard had told him the charges against him were false and that he was not in any combat or military unit. He cited Hubbard as telling him Russian soldiers had simply grabbed him from his house.
Putin decided to release him this week on ‘humanitarian grounds’, according to Russian news agency TASS.
The prisoner release comes amid a detente between Washington and Moscow as Trump turns his ire back to Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky.
Speaking to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, the US president seized the opportunity to pile more pressure onto Ukraine to cut a deal with Russia and end the four-year conflict.
“We want Zelensky to make a deal,” he said. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”
The rift with Kyiv has was blown open by Trump’s October 9 announcement that he would lift sanctions on Moscow to allow for diesel exports in a bid to help lower prices in the US ahead of the November midterm elections.
Since the announcement, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelensky said that a meeting with Witkoff in Oslo on Tuesday had reached an agreement to resolve the issues.
Despite the apparently cordial nature of the Oslo summit, Trump remains frustrated with Zelensky, whom he has repeatedly rebuked and suggested needs to be replaced.
Putin, who has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims, said on Wednesday that Russia would be open to restoring full economic ties with the US, in a sign of the deepening relationship with Trump.
He also suggested Russia could supply fertilisers in a larger amount the US.
Witkoff said he hoped that Putin would at least consider the resumption of trilateral talks with Washington and Kyiv, after the last round in Geneva in February came to nothing.
He said the talks this week in Oslo had been productive and that there was a basis for a ceasefire, according to Russian media.
Who is Stephen Hubbard?
Hubbard was placed in custody in 2022 after Russia captured Izyum, the city in Ukraine where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.
Local journalists have not been able to independently establish the circumstances of his capture, but his sister Patricia Hubbard Fox said she recognised her brother from a YouTube video.
The clip, which was recorded in an unknown location, appeared to show Mr Hubbard being questioned about his views on Putin and the war. Another video showed him with his hands bound, being struck with a sandal.
Fox said in 2024 that Hubbard was living off his pension and had few connections with local people – but the siblings haven’t spoken since September 2021.
Why was Stephen Hubbard imprisoned?
A Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary during a closed trial in October 2024. He was sentenced to six years and 10 months in prison.
Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised 1,000 US Dollars (around £747.83) a month.
State-owned media reported that Hubbard had pleaded guilty to the charges, but Fox argued that he held pro-Russian views and was unlikely to have taken up arms given his age.
Hubbard’s legal team argued that the charges were false and that soldiers had grabbed him from his home.
The US government under the Biden administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained. But The State Department has said Russia refused to grant US officials consular access.
The New York Times reported in February 2025 that Hubbard had been moved through at least five Russian detention centres before his trial.

Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired US schoolteacher from Michigan who was accused of joining the Ukrainian armed forces and held by Russia since the beginning of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, has been freed in what is being framed as a goodwill gesture from the Kremlin.
Russian President Vladimir Putin announced Hubbard's release on October 21 as be began his latest round of talks -- their ninth meeting -- with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg, which focused on negotiating an end to the war in Ukraine.
Putin said Hubbard, the only US prisoner held by Russia with the designation by Washington as "wrongfully detained," was at St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport, where he will fly back to the United States with Witkoff.
Witkoff framed Hubbard's release as a goodwill gesture from the Kremlin, calling Putin a "humanitarian."
"You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again," he told Putin.
Shortly afterward, US President Donald Trump confirmed Hubbard's release, saying he would soon be reunited with his family. "Welcome home, Stephen. It's great to have you back," he wrote on Truth Social.
Trump said he had "requested" Hubbard's release during a phone call with Putin last week and that Washington "was not required to give anything in return," describing the Kremlin's move as "unprecedented."
An official from the US State Department told RFE/RL that "Mr. Hubbard’s release was not part of an exchange, and no other concessions were provided."
"The Russian government made the unilateral decision to release Mr. Hubbard," the official said.
Following the latest call between the US and Russian presidents, Trump announced a deal to encourage Russian diesel exports and waived sanctions that were due to be imposed under a law he signed last month. Kyiv and its Western allies had warned these developments could further fuel Moscow's war machine.
Hubbard was detained by Russian forces in April 2022. He was later sentenced by the Moscow City Court in October 2024 to six years and 10 months in prison on charges of being a mercenary.
Russian prosecutors claimed he had fought for Ukraine's territorial defense forces in the northeastern Kharkiv region, which was then heavily occupied by Russian forces, under a contract worth $1,000 per month.
Hubbard's family, particularly his sister Patricia Fox, had previously expressed doubts about the accusations, stating Hubbard had long been sympathetic to Russia and had moved to Ukraine in 2014.
Fox revealed Hubbard had lived in the city of Izyum after splitting up with his Ukrainian girlfriend and was there when the war broke out. She also pointed to a video released in May 2022 in which Hubbard was seen commenting on the war.
In the video, he claimed to have witnessed Ukrainian forces shelling Izyum for "propaganda purposes" and expressed understanding for Putin's decision to invade Ukraine.
It remains unclear under what circumstances the video was made, raising questions about whether Hubbard was coerced into making the statements. There were no reports or official statements about his arrest or how he ended up in Moscow.
The subject of US citizens being held in Russian prisons has become a prominent political issue in recent years, with many viewing their cases as part of a broader pattern of Americans being used as leverage in wider geopolitical disputes.
Hubbard's release came ahead of November's US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress, and amid protracted negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv to end Russia's full-scale invasion.
The two sides remain far apart on the terms of a potential settlement, with the Kremlin offering no concessions and sticking to its hard-line demands.
Under Trump, as well as his predecessor, Joe Biden, Moscow and Washington conducted several major swaps of prisoners held in US and Russian prisons. But Moscow still holds several US citizens whose cases have yet to be resolved.
According to Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer at Global Reach, an advocacy group, who spoke with RFE/RL earlier this year, at least five Americans remain in Russian detention. Other reports put the number as high as 10.
"We are grateful to the Trump Administration for reuniting Stephen Hubbard with his family," Lebson said in a statement on October 21. "But at the same time, we know that there are five other families of Americans held in Russia who are going to have a hard time understanding why their loved one was not included in the deal."

LONDON -- Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan who had been in Russian detention since 2022, was released Wednesday.
President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Russia to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and oversee Hubbard's release. Witkoff landed in the Russian city of St. Petersburg on Wednesday morning, a Kremlin aide confirmed, ahead of the planned meeting with Putin.
Trump's envoy thanked Putin for freeing Hubbard, according to a readout of the meeting published by the Kremlin. Putin said that Hubbard -- who was detained in eastern Ukraine in April 2022 -- was taken to St. Peterburg's Pulkovo Airport, the readout said.
"I want to thank you very much. The president sends his thanks," Witkoff said. "Because of you, he's going home to his family."
"You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian," Witkoff told Putin. "You are a humanitarian also, sir."
Hubbard's sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, told ABC News on Wednesday that she was thanking Trump "for being the hand of God and bringing Stephen Hubbard home."
"He's been gone a long, long time. Thank you President Trump for caring for everyday Americans," she said, adding that the development was "awesome" and that the "Lord has given me peace."
Fox said she had not yet spoken to her brother or to U.S. officials and that she learned about Hubbard's release from the media. Hubbard, she added, will be flown to San Antonio where there is a military base that released Americans are usually brought to for treatment.
Trump later wrote in a post to social media he asked Putin to release Hubbard in a phone call that took place last week. "Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family," Trump wrote.
The U.S. "was not required to give anything in return -- an unprecedented situation for Russia," Trump added. "There was no 'swap' necessary for this release."
The president then posted to social media again defending his recent decision to waive numerous sanctions on Russia.
"If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt," Trump wrote of the discussions over Hubbard's release.
Witkoff arrived in St. Petersburg as the Trump administration was closing in on a deal that would see multiple Americans released from detention in Russia, two U.S. officials and another source familiar with the matter told ABC News.
The talks were centered on Hubbard and several other U.S. citizens held by Moscow on what the administration believes are dubious charges, the source said.
Hubbard had been living in eastern Ukraine as a civilian since around 2014, where he taught English and had a relationship with a Ukrainian woman, according to his family.
After he was detained, Russian authorities charged Hubbard with acting as a mercenary and fighting for Ukraine, sentencing him to nearly seven years in prison. Hubbard's family and U.S. officials said the charges were false and the State Department designated him as wrongfully detained.
During their meeting, Witkoff and Putin discussed the latest U.S.-led efforts to end Moscow's ongoing invasion, which the Kremlin launched in February 2022.
"One thing that I hope to accomplish today is to have some good conversation between us about resumption potentially of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States," Witkoff said.
Witkoff also touted U.S.-Russian "business and economic cooperation" as "an example of what the possibilities are in the future."
Witkoff traveled to St. Petersburg following a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Norwegian capital of Oslo on Tuesday. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also attended the talks, which focused on ceasefire proposals to halt Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Witkoff's latest round of shuttle diplomacy comes amid intensifying White House pressure on Zelenskyy to make concessions to secure a peace deal with Moscow.
In recent weeks, Trump waived a raft of sanctions on Moscow and again blamed Kyiv for the lack of progress in U.S.-sponsored peace talks, even suggesting that Zelenskyy should be replaced as Ukrainian president.
On Tuesday, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that the U.S. had received "nothing" for its support of Ukraine.
"Look, we have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We've got nothing back other than high diesel," Trump said. "We have given, probably, possibly, more money to Ukraine than almost anybody over the years, hundreds of billions of dollars. We've got nothing back, and the American taxpayers are tired of it. We want Zelenskyy to make a deal."
Following his meetings in Oslo on Tuesday, Zelenskyy said in posts to social media that he was "thankful to the American side" for its input on propose future security guarantees for Kyiv. The Ukrainian president also said he spoke with Secretary of State Marco Rubio by phone to discuss "sensitive issues such as Starlink, ballistic missile interceptors and intelligence."
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said he continued to hold meetings in Oslo. "A lot depends on whether the American side manages to hear something new from Russia today -- about peace, not about continuing the war," he wrote.
ABC News' Joe Simonetti, Shannon K. Kingston, Fritz Farrow, Nicholas Kerr, Emily Chang, Anna Sergeeva and Justin Gomez contributed to this report.
